notes.b: Fat is eaten mostly as triglycerides, which are too big to absorb. Digestion is hydrolysis, the splitting of a molecule using water, done by enzymes (specific biological catalysts that work at about 37 °C), and lipase is the enzyme that does this for fat.
points: A triglyceride is one glycerol molecule bonded to three fatty acid chains by ester bonds, so there are three bonds for the enzyme to break.

Lipase hydrolyses the ester bonds of triglycerides, splitting them into fatty acids and glycerol. Monoglycerides and diglycerides (glycerol with one or two fatty acids still attached) form as intermediate products on the way.

Fats do not dissolve in water, so lipase can act only at the surface of a fat droplet, and a larger droplet surface area speeds digestion. This is why fat must be emulsified (broken into tiny droplets) first.
Diagram: a triglyceride showing one glycerol backbone and three fatty acid chains, with the ester bonds labelled.
notes.tip: The product column in an exam table is always fatty acids and glycerol. Give both, and name lipase as the enzyme.

notes.h: Mouth and stomach: little fat digestion
notes.b: Very little fat is digested before it reaches the small intestine, so the early stages of the canal matter mainly for how long fat stays in them.
points: The mouth carries out little or no lipid digestion.
Gastric lipase (lipase made in the stomach) hydrolyses only a small proportion of the triglycerides.
Fat slows the emptying of the stomach, so it stays there for longer than carbohydrate or protein, which is why a fatty meal keeps you feeling full.
notes.tip: For a long answer tracing fat through the digestive system, state that little digestion happens before the small intestine.

notes.h: Bile: where it comes from and what it contains
notes.b: Bile is a digestive secretion that works on fat without being an enzyme. Knowing where it is made, stored and released helps you place it correctly in the sequence.
points: The liver produces bile, which is stored and concentrated in the gall bladder and released through the bile duct into the duodenum (the first part of the small intestine).
Bile contains bile salts and bile pigments such as bilirubin, and it contains no enzymes, so it cannot chemically digest fat.
Diagram: the liver, gall bladder, bile duct, pancreas, pancreatic duct and duodenum, with the flow of bile and pancreatic juice labelled.
notes.tip: Bile is made in the liver, not the stomach or pancreas, and it is stored in the gall bladder, not made there. Never write that bile is an enzyme or that it digests fat.

notes.b: Bile does three jobs, and the most important is preparing fat for lipase. Emulsification is a physical change, not a chemical one.
points: Bile salts emulsify fat, breaking large fat globules into very small droplets. An emulsion is tiny droplets of one liquid dispersed in another, and no bonds are broken, so this is not hydrolysis.
Emulsification increases the surface area of the fat, so lipase can act on far more of it at once.
Bile is alkaline, so it neutralises the acid chyme (the partly digested food) arriving from the stomach and creates a suitable pH for the pancreatic and intestinal enzymes to work.
Bile also carries waste products such as bilirubin out of the body.
notes.tip: Three functions of bile come up: emulsify fat, neutralise the acid chyme, and remove waste. Keep the word emulsify for bile; what lipase does is hydrolysis.

notes.h: Small intestine: lipid digestion is completed
notes.b: Most fat is digested in the small intestine, where lipase from two sources meets fat that bile has already emulsified.
points: Pancreas (acting in the duodenum): it secretes pancreatic juice containing lipase. The substrate is triglycerides in the emulsified droplets, and the products are fatty acids and glycerol.
Small intestine: its wall secretes intestinal juice containing lipase, which acts on the same substrate, triglycerides, to give fatty acids and glycerol.
Liver and gall bladder: they supply bile, which has no enzyme and emulsifies fat into droplets.
Lipase hydrolyses triglycerides into fatty acids and glycerol, with some monoglycerides and diglycerides as intermediate products.
notes.tip: In the table question, give both rows: pancreatic juice with lipase, and intestinal juice with lipase. The product is fatty acids and glycerol each time.

notes.b: The digested fat is absorbed through the villi, the finger-like projections of the small intestine wall. Each villus has a capillary network and a lacteal (a lymph capillary), and the route a product takes depends on its size.
points: Short-chain fatty acids and glycerol are small and water-soluble, so they pass directly into the capillaries of the villi and do not need to be rebuilt. The hepatic portal vein carries them to the liver.
Long-chain fatty acids and monoglycerides diffuse into the cells lining the villi, where they are rebuilt into triglycerides. Fat is therefore not absorbed as whole triglycerides.
The triglycerides are coated with protein (and other lipids) to form chylomicrons, which are too large to enter the capillaries.
Chylomicrons pass into the lacteals, the lymph capillaries at the centre of each villus.

Lymph carries the chylomicrons through the lymphatic system into the thoracic duct, which empties into the blood near the heart. The fat reaches the general circulation without first passing through the liver; the liver later removes what is left of the chylomicrons from the blood.
Diagram: a villus cross-section showing the capillary network, the lacteal and the two routes.
notes.tip: Do not say all fat goes by the lacteal or all by the portal vein: the lacteal carries the long-chain fat, and the capillaries carry the short-chain products.

notes.h: Route of fat through the alimentary canal
notes.b: Tracing a fat molecule from the mouth to the blood brings the stages together in order.
points: 1. Mouth and stomach: little or no lipid digestion takes place.
2. Duodenum: bile emulsifies the fat and pancreatic lipase hydrolyses it.
3. Villi: the products are absorbed. Long-chain fat enters the lacteals, while short-chain products enter the capillaries.
4. Lymphatic system: lymph carries the fat from the lacteals into the thoracic duct and then into the bloodstream.
5. Hepatic portal vein: carries the short-chain fatty acids and glycerol, absorbed directly into the capillaries, to the liver.
6. General circulation: the blood distributes fat around the body.
Diagram: the digestive system, labelled mouth, stomach, liver, gall bladder, pancreas, small intestine and hepatic portal vein.
notes.tip: Long answers on tracing fat earn marks for each secretion with its job, so name the secretion and say what it does at each stage.

notes.b: Once absorbed, fat is moved around the body, broken down again at the tissues and either used for energy or stored.
points: Lipids travel in the blood as lipoproteins (lipids packed with protein): chylomicrons carry dietary fat, and very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) carry fat made in the liver.
Lipoprotein lipase, an enzyme at the body tissues, hydrolyses the triglycerides in lipoproteins into fatty acids and glycerol, which the cells take up.
Muscle cells oxidise fatty acids in respiration to release energy. Fat is the most concentrated energy source, giving 37 kJ (9 kcal) per gram.
Glycerol is converted into glucose in the liver or enters glycolysis (the first stage of respiration).
Surplus fatty acids are rebuilt into triglycerides and stored in adipose (fat) tissue under the skin and around organs, which gives insulation, protection of organs and an energy reserve.
The liver converts surplus carbohydrate (and protein) into fatty acids and triglycerides, which it exports as VLDL.
notes.tip: Higher Level answers on utilisation should include lipoproteins, lipase at the tissues, oxidation for energy, storage in adipose tissue, and glycerol to glucose.

keyTerms.definition: A lipid made of one glycerol molecule bonded to three fatty acid chains.
The enzyme that hydrolyses the ester bonds of triglycerides into fatty acids and glycerol.
An alkaline fluid made by the liver, stored in the gall bladder and released into the duodenum to emulsify fat.
The breaking of large fat globules into very small droplets, which increases the surface area for lipase.
The compounds in bile that emulsify fat in the small intestine.
A droplet of triglyceride coated with protein, formed in the villi and carried in lymph.
A lymph capillary at the centre of each villus that absorbs fat.
A particle of lipid and protein that transports fats in the blood.
The three-carbon alcohol that forms the backbone of a triglyceride.

questions.prompt: Outline how dietary fat is emulsified and digested in the small intestine. Name the secretions involved and state the role of each.
questions.model: Bile from the liver, stored in the gall bladder and released into the duodenum, contains bile salts that emulsify fat into very small droplets, increasing its surface area. Bile is alkaline and neutralises acid chyme. Pancreatic juice from the pancreas and intestinal juice from the wall of the small intestine contain lipase, which hydrolyses triglycerides into fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.prompt: Trace the route of dietary fat from the mouth to the body tissues. Name the organ, secretion, enzyme, substrate and product at each digestive stage, explain how the products are absorbed and carried through the body, and describe how the liver and body tissues use the absorbed fat.
questions.model: Mouth and stomach: little fat digestion; gastric lipase hydrolyses a small proportion of triglycerides. Small intestine: liver produces bile, stored in gall bladder, released into duodenum; bile salts emulsify fat, increasing surface area; bile is alkaline and neutralises chyme. Pancreatic juice and intestinal juice contain lipase, which hydrolyses triglycerides to fatty acids and glycerol. Absorption: short-chain fatty acids and glycerol enter the villus capillaries and the hepatic portal vein; long-chain fatty acids and monoglycerides are rebuilt into triglycerides in the villus cells, coated with protein to form chylomicrons, and enter the lacteals. Lymph carries chylomicrons through the thoracic duct into the blood. Liver: processes absorbed fats and produces VLDL. Body tissues: lipoprotein lipase releases fatty acids and glycerol; muscle cells oxidise fatty acids in respiration for energy; glycerol is converted to glucose or enters glycolysis; surplus fat is stored in adipose tissue.
